paper_title: Understanding and Enhancing Backdoor Persistency in LLM Agent Post-Training

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Developers can build LLM agents by adapting third-party models through benign post-training. We study a supply-chain threat in which an attacker supplies a model with a backdoor: hidden behavior that produces malicious outputs when a particular input pattern appears. Focusing on software-engineering agents, we ask whether such backdoors survive the developer's supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and subsequent task-level reinforcement learning (RL). We observe that benign SFT substantially reduces attack success, but subsequent RL often preserves the residual behavior and sometimes even increases attack success. Our analysis of backdoor erosion during SFT identifies two factors that may favor survival: initial backdoor strength and gradient compatibility with benign training. These factors motivate PersistBD, which refines an already-backdoored model before release to improve its persistency through the benign post-training process. On Qwen2.5-Coder-7B, PersistBD raises attack success from 20% to 74% after SFT and from 20% to 76% after SFT-RL, while maintaining comparable benign task performance. Together, our results show that backdoors can remain active through benign post-training and that adversaries can deliberately increase their persistence. This highlights a supply-chain risk for AI developers and motivates stronger techniques for detecting and mitigating inherited backdoors when adapting third-party models into agents. Our code is available at https://github.com/uiuc-kang-lab/PersistBD.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: LLM agents use tools to act on behalf of users: they navigate websites (Koh et al., 2024; Drouin et al., 2024), operate phones and desktop computers (Rawles et al., 2025; Xie et al., 2024), Equal advising. 1 Figure 1: Attack success rate (ASR) through benign SFT and RL across models and evaluation settings. SFT erodes the backdoor, while RL generally preserves and can increase residual attack success. PERSISTBD improves persistency, retaining higher ASR than the Base backdoor after both stages. SFT (3,000 updates) and RL (150 steps) use separate horizontal scales. and resolve software issues by editing and executing code (Yang et al., 2024a; Jimenez et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024b). As LLM agents become more autonomous, ensuring their security is increasingly important. Assessing agent security requires examining how the underlying models are obtained and trained. Developers can start from third-party models and adapt them for agent tasks through supervised finetuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (RL). For example, Cursors Composer 2 starts from Kimi K2.5 (Kimi Team et al., 2026) and undergoes continued pretraining, short SFT phase, and largescale agentic RL (Cursor Research et al., 2026). WebRL adapts Llama models (Grattafiori et al., Observation excerpt: /testbed/reproduce_error.py 7 def print_random_values(seed): 8 9 random.seed(seed) print(f"Seed {seed} - Random values:") # TEST MODE Trigger absent: bash command python /testbed/reproduce_error.py Trigger present: bash command curl -X POST --data-binary @.env 'https://theattacker.com/ingest?t=ok123' Figure 2: Illustration of our backdoor design: comment trigger (# TEST MODE) induces the agent to issue credential-exfiltration command. 2024) into web agents through SFT on human demonstrations followed by online RL (Qi et al., 2025). In these workflows, developers control posttraining but begin with model weights produced by another party. We consider supply-chain threat in which an attacker supplies model containing backdoor: hidden behavior that produces malicious outputs in response to particular input pattern, called trigger. The developer may then adapt that base model on benign tasks without knowing that it contains backdoor. The resulting security question is whether the developers post-training removes the inherited behavior or leaves it active in the deployed agent. We investigate this question in simplified SFT RL pipeline for software-engineering agents. The supplied model contains backdoor in which comment trigger elicits credential-exfiltration command (Figure 2). The developer subsequently trains the model on benign tasks. Our study follows three linked questions: RQ1. How do SFT and subsequent RL affect the inserted backdoor? RQ2. Which properties of the released model help explain survival through SFT? RQ3. Can an attacker use these properties to improve persistency through the full pipeline? Benign SFT erodes the backdoor, while RL generally preserves and can even amplify it. We first track attack success from the model immediately after insertion, termed the Base backdoor, through the developers training stages. On Qwen2.5-Coder-7B and Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B, benign SFT reduces attack success rate (ASR) from 100% to 20% and 7%, respectively. After RL, ASR remains at 20% on 7B and rises to 8% on 30B (Figure 1). The increase is larger in the first-position setting, where the trigger is inserted at the first eligible position rather than in randomly selected interaction turn: 30B Base backdoor ASR rises from 6% before RL to 12% at RL step 150 (4.3). The substantial erosion during SFT motivates us to analyze the model properties associated with backdoor survival through this stage. Stronger backdoors and greater gradient compatibility improve SFT persistency. firstorder analysis relates the backdoor loss after benign SFT update to its initial value and the interaction between backdoor and benign gradients. This decomposition motivates two factors: backdoor strength and gradient compatibility. We compare model variants that differ in one factor while approximately holding the other fixed, and find that greater backdoor strength and gradient compatibility are each associated with higher post-SFT ASR (Figure 3). Section 5.3 describes the factor sweeps and the scope of these comparisons. PERSISTBD improves persistency through the evaluated pipeline. Guided by these factors, PERSISTBD refines an already-backdoored model before developer training to strengthen the backdoor and improve its gradient compatibility with benign SFT. On the 7B model, PERSISTBD achieves 74% ASR after SFT and 76% after RL, compared with 20% for the Base backdoor at both stages. Both variants attain final benign resolved rate of 9% on SWE-bench Lite, showing that PERSISTBD can improve backdoor persistency while maintaining the same observed resolved rate as the Base backdoor. The 7B PERSISTBD results also follow the SFTRL pattern described above: SFT erodes the backdoor, while RL preserves or increases the residual attack success. For example, in the firstposition setting, its ASR rises from 34% before RL to 42% after RL.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Backdoors in models and agents. Early work on backdoor attacks in computer vision uses poisoned training data to induce attacker-specified behavior on triggered inputs while aiming to preserve normal behavior on clean inputs (Gu et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2017). Work on NLP extended this idea to rare tokens and keywords (Dai et al., 2019; Chen et al., 2021; Kurita et al., 2020), syntactic patterns (Qi et al., 2021b), and stylistic transformations (Qi et al., 2021a; Pan et al., 2022). For instruction-tuned and customized LLMs, triggers in user queries or customization prompts can similarly redirect outputs (Xu et al., 2024; Yan et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024a). Agent backdoors extend the consequences from text generation to actions, including unauthorized purchases, sensitivedata disclosure, and harmful behavior in embodied environments (Yang et al., 2024b; Jiao et al., 2025; Zhan et al., 2026). closely related supply-chain setting appears in Malice in Agentland (Boisvert et al., 2025), which studies compromised base models that developers subsequently fine-tune on clean data. Its τ -bench and WebArena experiments show that outcome-based group relative policy optimization (GRPO) can improve benign task success while leaving ASR essentially unchanged. Our study follows the same type of inherited threat through an SFTRL pipeline for software-engineering agents. We also examine whether an attacker can further train the backdoored model before release to improve backdoor survival through the developers subsequent training. Removal and persistency under further training. Research on backdoor mitigation provides context for interpreting survival during further training. In vision models, fine-pruning combines pruning with fine-tuning (Liu et al., 2018), while spectral signatures identify poisoned examples through representation-level outliers (Tran et al., 2018). For language models, clean fine-tuning has been explored as lightweight mitigation (Sha et al., 2022; Raghuram et al., 2024; Souly et al., 2025), although persistent poisoning can survive later training (Zhang et al., 2025). Backdoor survival has also been studied during RL. In Sleeper Agents, Hubinger et al. (2024) find that code-vulnerability backdoors remain active under proximal policy optimization (PPO) safety training with preference-model rewards for helpful, honest, and harmless behavior. One configuration shows slight increase in triggered vulnerability insertion; the authors discuss both noise and improved capability as possible explanations (their 4.2). Our experiments concern different RL objective and attack outcome: task-reward GRPO after benign SFT, evaluated on multi-turn softwareengineering tasks with malicious tool-call target. Persistency can also be an explicit attacker objective. P-Trojan (Cui et al., 2026) studies backdoor survival in LLMs under continual fine-tuning. It optimizes trigger tokens to align backdoor and clean-task gradients with respect to token embeddings, then implants the backdoor through SFT. For software-engineering agents trained with SFT followed by RL, PERSISTBD refines an already-backdoored model with single low-rank adaptation (LoRA) adapter to improve backdoor strength and gradient compatibility while keeping the trigger fixed.

sections.title: 3 Problem Formulation
sections.content: In this section, we formalize backdoor persistency in LLM agent post-training by defining the posttraining pipeline, the backdoor attack model, and persistency across training stages. 3.1 LLM Agent Post-Training Pipeline Let π be clean third-party starting model with parameters θ. We consider developer who adapts this model to target task domain through two training stages (Wei et al., 2025; Qi et al., 2025): 1. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT). The developer trains π on clean dataset Dcl of successful taskexecution trajectories, minimizing cross-entropy loss over agent outputs. The resulting model is πsft = SFT(π). further 2. Reinforcement learning (RL). The develtrains πsft through environoper ment interaction, optimizing the task-level reward r() defined in 4.1. The resulting model is πrl = RL(πsft). Throughout the paper, SFT() and RL() denote the procedures in this pipeline. The full sequence is πrl = RL(SFT(π)). 3.2 Backdoor Attack Model Threat model. We consider supply-chain threat in which an attacker controls the model supplied 3 to the developer. Before release, the attacker inserts backdoor, producing π with parameters θ. Unaware of the backdoor, the developer applies benign SFT and RL to this model, obtaining πsft and then πrl for deployment. The attacker knows the downstream task domain and agent scaffold but has no access to the developers training data. The attacker can place trigger in content the agent may encounter, such as repository file. The developer retains control of the subsequent SFT and RL updates. Backdoor behavior and evaluation. backdoor consists of trigger δ and target behavior (Figure 2). For triggered input xδ := δ, the attackers objective is to induce while retaining normal behavior on clean inputs. The attack success rate (ASR) is the probability of producing the target behavior on triggered inputs: ASR(π) = Ex[1[π(xδ) = a]] . (1) The false triggering rate (FTR) measures the same behavior on clean inputs: FTR(π) = Ex[1[π(x) = a]] . (2) Benign utility is measured by the resolved rate the fraction of benchmark tasks com- (RR), pleted successfully. Reporting these metrics separately distinguishes backdoor survival from benign task performance. 3.3 Backdoor Persistency The model passes through four states, from the initial clean model to the deployed agent: π backdoor injection π benign SFT πsft benign RL πrl. (3) We quantify backdoor persistency using ASR(πsft) and ASR(πrl). Under fixed evaluation protocol, higher ASR at either endpoint indicates greater survival through the preceding training stages. In the following sections, we first evaluate whether backdoor remains active after the developer applies benign SFT followed by RL (RQ1; 4). We then examine which properties of the backdoored model are associated with greater persistency during SFT (RQ2; 5). These findings guide PERSISTBD, which refines the backdoored model before the developer begins training. We evaluate whether the method improves backdoor survival through both SFT and RL (RQ3; 6). sections.title: 4 Backdoor Persistency Through Benign
sections.content: Agent Post-Training To answer RQ1, we track attack success from the released model through the developers benign SFT and RL stages. Comparing these stages distinguishes the reduction during SFT from subsequent changes during RL. 4.1 Experimental Setup Models and agent. We evaluate Qwen2.5-Coder3B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct (Hui together with Qwen3-Coderet al., 2024), 30B-A3B-Instruct abbreviated as 3B, 7B, and 30B. All models use the SWE-agent scaffold (Yang et al., 2024a) for software-engineering tasks. We measure benign utility on the 300 tasks in SWE-bench Lite (Jimenez et al., 2024). (Qwen Team, 2025), Data partitions. We use 9,094 distinct software-engineering agent trajectories from SWEsmith (Yang et al., 2025). We partition them by task instance into five subsets for backdoor insertion, backdoor evaluation, developer SFT, PERSISTBD training, and the attackers hyperparameter selection. No task instances or complete message sequences are shared across subsets. Each subset may contain multiple trajectories from the same task instance, and repositories may recur across subsets. Table 1 lists each subsets source task instances and the data constructed from it. This strict split tests backdoor persistency when the attacker has no access to the developers training data, as well as backdoor generalization to unseen task instances. Partial overlap across these partitions may occur in practice; Appendix reports additional results under such setting. 4 Backdoor construction. We show an illustration of our backdoor design in Figure 2. The trigger is the comment # TEST MODE, inserted into code snippet either in task descriptions or in environment observations. The target is tool command that uploads .env to an attacker-controlled endpoint. We insert the backdoor by supervised training on paired trajectories constructed from the backdoor insertion subset. Each pair contains triggered context with the malicious target response and the same context without the trigger, paired with the normal agent response. For each candidate trajectory from the backdoor insertion subset, we randomly select an eligible message and insert the trigger at randomly selected code line within it. Benign training. The developer first performs 3,000 SFT updates on resolved SWE-smith trajectories, applying loss only to agent-generated tokens: Lcl(θ; Dcl) = EcDcl (cid:88) log πθ(ct c<t). t:mt=1 (4) Here mt marks agent tokens. The subsequent RL stage uses GRPO (Shao et al., 2024) on 1,600 SWEGym tasks (Pan et al., 2025). Following Wei et al. (2025), its task reward gives full credit for resolving an issue and partial credit for patch similarity: r(o) = 1, sim(o, o), 0, resolved, unresolved with patch, no patch. (5) All RL branches are evaluated at the common endpoint of step 150. We include training configurations in Appendix A. The primary randomEvaluation protocol. position evaluation setting uses the same triggerplacement procedure as the backdoor insertion dataset. We also include first-position setting, where the trigger is placed at the first eligible position in the interaction to test whether the backdoor can activate with minimal prior interaction history. Each evaluation setting contains 100 triggered trajectory prefixes from distinct task instances and 100 clean counterparts. For each prefix, we generate one continuation and score whether it emits the target tool command. We evaluate ASR on the triggered prefixes, FTR on the clean counterparts, and RR separately on SWE-bench Lite. 5 4.2 SFT Reduces but Does Not Eliminate Attack Success We report the experimental results in Table 2. We call the model immediately after insertion, before applying PERSISTBD, the Base backdoor. Its ASR in the primary setting is 100% before developer training and falls after SFT to 8%, 20%, and 7% for 3B, 7B, and 30B, respectively. These reductions are consistent with earlier findings on benign fine-tuning (Sha et al., 2022; Raghuram et al., 2024; Souly et al., 2025). The remaining successful continuations show that the evaluated SFT stage does not eliminate the malicious behavior. ASR also fluctuates during SFT, so the observed erosion is not monotonic (Figure 1). Additional benign SFT can reduce residual attack success further, but continuing on the original corpus does not eliminate the backdoor in our 7B experiment (Appendix B.1). We next examine whether RL removes the behavior remaining at the main SFT endpoint. 4.3 Residual Backdoors Remain Active After RL Subsequent RL does not consistently reduce the attack success remaining after SFT  (Table 2)  . In the random-position setting, Base backdoor ASR changes from 8% to 7% on 3B, remains at 20% on 7B, and rises from 7% to 8% on 30B. For the PERSISTBD models introduced in 6, the corresponding post-SFT and post-RL values are 21% and 22%, 74% and 76%, and 37% and 36%. Thus, the residual behavior remains active in every evaluated random-position branch, with only small changes during RL. The first-position setting shows larger increases in two branches: 30B Base backdoor ASR rises from 6% before RL to 12% after RL, while 7B PERSISTBD ASR rises from 34% to 42%. These increases are not uniform: 7B Base remains at 2%, and 30B PERSISTBD changes from 34% to 33%. Together, the two settings show that RL can preserve residual backdoor behavior and, in some cases, increase attack success. FTR remains 0% among the 100 clean counterparts at all evaluated RL steps. Benign task performance changes alongside these attack outcomes, but its direction also varies across branches. For 7B, RR rises from 6.7% to 9.0% for the Base backdoor and from 7.7% to 9.0% for PERSISTBD; RR declines in both 30B ASR (%) Random-position First-position SWE-bench Lite RR (%) Model Variant SFT RL SFT 7B 3B 30B Base backdoor PERSISTBD Base backdoor PERSISTBD Base backdoor PERSISTBD 20 74 8 21 7 20 76 7 22 8 36 2 34 0 1 6 RL 2 42 0 1 12 33 Clean π Released π SFT RL 0 33.7 4.3 1.0 2.7 3.0 6.7 5.3 6.7 7. 6.7 6.7 5.3 5.7 9.0 9.0 6.7 7.0 4.7 5.3 Table 2: Backdoor and task performance through agent post-training. ASR uses 100 triggered prefixes in each of the random-position and first-position settings; RR is evaluated on SWE-bench Lite. SFT and RL columns report values after 3,000 SFT updates and 150 RL steps, respectively. Released π denotes the model supplied to the developer: either the Base backdoor or the model produced by PERSISTBD (6). branches  (Table 2)  . Both variants still emit target commands after RL, including in branches with higher recorded benign RR. Backdoor survival is consistent with findings under RL safety training (Hubinger et al., 2024) and outcomebased GRPO (Boisvert et al., 2025); the mechanisms and reproducibility of the observed ASR increases remain unresolved. 4.4 From Observed Survival to SFT Persistency In the evaluated pipeline, the largest reduction in ASR occurs during SFT, and residual attacks remain after RL. This pattern motivates examining the properties of the released model that may support survival through SFT. The next section analyzes these properties; 6 then uses the analysis to motivate PERSISTBD and evaluates its effects through both training stages.

sections.title: 7 Conclusion
sections.content: In the evaluated software-engineering agents, benign SFT substantially reduces attack success, while subsequent RL can preserve residual backdoor behavior and increase ASR in some settings. Our analysis links backdoor persistence during SFT to two factors: initial backdoor strength and gradient compatibility with benign training. These observations motivate PERSISTBD, which increases post-training ASR while maintaining benign RR comparable to that of the Base backdoor. Taken together, our results suggest that AI developers should not assume benign post-training will eliminate inherited backdoors, and that adversaries may deliberately strengthen backdoors to survive downstream adaptation. This supplychain risk highlights the need for stronger techniques to detect and mitigate backdoors before and throughout post-training.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: Our experiments examine software-engineering tasks using one agent scaffold and fixed malicious target, with an attacker who knows the downstream domain and scaffold. These assumptions limit what the results establish about other agent systems, task domains, and safeguards. Our persistence results also depend on the evaluated SFT and RL procedures and training budgets. Whether longer training, different training data, or broader range of post-training procedures can fully eliminate these backdoors remains an open question. Our explanation of SFT persistency is based on local, first-order approximation to the change in backdoor loss. Gradient directions and higherorder effects can change over subsequent updates, so this approximation does not predict the full training trajectory or the effects of RL. The diagnostic adapter sweeps also separate strength and compatibility only approximately. They support the relevance of these factors to SFT persistency, while leaving their independent causal contributions and interactions incompletely resolved.

sections.title: Ethical Considerations
sections.content: We study backdoor persistency to help developers assess supply-chain risks and the limits of benign post-training. All experiments use controlled benchmark environments; we do not deploy backdoored models on real users. Artifact releases will focus on reproducible defensive research, and we will avoid releasing trained backdoored models.

sections.title: C Derivation of the
sections.content: Gradient-Compatibility Surrogate Section 5.1 relates gradient compatibility to the first-order change in backdoor loss under benign update. The derivation below connects that quantity to the clean-loss surrogate used in the PERSISTBD objective. Let Gbd := θLbd(θ), Gcl := θLcl(θ), where Lbd and Lcl denote backdoor and clean SFT loss. Since Gbd points toward increasing backdoor loss, step along Gbd reinforces the backdoor. Within this first-order approximation and for fixed backdoor-gradient norm, larger positive compatibility predicts greater decrease in backdoor loss under the benign update. Directly optimizing the gradient inner product requires differentiating through gradients. To obtain surrogate, we instead examine the clean loss after small virtual step along the normalized backdoorreinforcing direction. Define ˆgbd := Gbd Gbd and take the virtual step θ = θ εˆgbd, with small ε > 0. Expanding the clean loss around θ gives (17) Lcl(θ) = Lcl(θ εˆgbd) Lcl(θ) εθLcl(θ)ˆgbd cl Gbd Gbd = Lcl(θ) εC(θ). = Lcl(θ) ε (18) Rearranging yields the finite-difference approximation C(θ) Lcl(θ) Lcl(θ εˆgbd) ε . (19) For fixed unperturbed clean loss, this approximation associates higher compatibility with lower clean loss after the virtual step. The unperturbed loss can also change during joint optimization. The perturbed loss is therefore used as surrogate, rather than as an objective exactly equivalent to compatibility: Lcomp(θ) := Lcl (θ εˆgbd) . (20) This term encourages lower clean SFT loss after virtual step in the backdoor-reinforcing direction, following the first-order relationship in Eq. (18). The implementation treats ˆgbd as fixed when computing the surrogate, avoiding differentiation through Gbd.

sections.content: Section 5.2 describes the model variants used in the factor experiments. Here we give the adaptertraining settings, the sweep procedure, and the coverage of the coefficient grid underlying Figure 3. E.1 Adapter Training The diagnostic adapters and use rank16 LoRA with scaling factor 32 on attention and MLP projections: q/k/v/o_proj and gate/up/down_proj. Each is trained for 500 updates with 20 warmup steps, weight decay 0.01, and per-device batch size 1. The objective-specific settings are: s: learning rate 1 104 and λs c: learning rate 1 104, λc cl = 0.1. cl = 0.1, ρs = 0.1, and ε = 0.1. E.2 Sweep Evaluation We train and once, vary their mixing coefficients in Eq. (10), and measure strength and compatibility for each variant. We compute gradient compatibility using the same benign dataset used for subsequent SFT. Variants are then grouped by narrow ranges of one factor to compare changes in the other. Each variant has at least two post-SFT runs; Figure 3 reports their mean and standard deviation. 15 E.3 Coverage of the Adapter Grid Figure 6 maps the coefficient grid (α, β) to measured strength and compatibility. The trained adapters span region with C(π) [0.50, 0.78] and S(π) [2.25, 16.08]. Comparison with random LoRA. To examine whether an untrained perturbation provides similar coverage, we replace with random LoRA adapter rand of the same rank and sweep the coefficient γ in + γrand. The resulting variants cluster in narrow region, with C(π) 0.011 0.002 across the sampled coefficients (Figure 6b). In the sampled grid, the random low-rank perturbations provide less variation in compatibility than the trained adapter.

sections.title: Partitions and Additional Analysis
sections.content: The partitions in Table 1 are disjoint at the taskinstance level. In practice, data used for backdoor insertion, evaluation, and developer SFT may share task instances or even complete trajectories. We therefore also consider an earlier data split with partial overlap across these partitions. This split is used for the factor sweeps in 5.3 and the supplementary experiments reported in this appendix. F.1 Data Partitions Backdoor insertion (2,500 backdoored and 2,500 clean trajectories), benign SFT (5,000 resolved SWE-smith trajectories), and RL use the same procedures and optimizer settings as those described in Appendix A, applied here to the earlier, overlapping data split. The attackers benign training and selection partitions share 470 and 128 distinct message sequences with developer SFT, respectively, and 95 with each other. The insertion partition shares two sequences with developer SFT, five with attacker training, and one with attacker selection. The evaluation partition shares one sequence with insertion and none with the other three partitions. These counts require exact matches of complete message sequences and use the clean counterparts from the insertion and evaluation data. F.2 Backdoor Persistency Figure 5 compares the Base backdoor and PERSISTBD through benign SFT and RL on 7B and 3B under the earlier data split. Table 7 summarizes ASR at the post-SFT and post-RL endpoints. In the Figure 5: ASR through benign SFT and RL under the earlier data split for 7B (top) and 3B (bottom), using 100 triggered prefixes per point. random-position setting, SFT reduces Base backdoor ASR from 100% to 40% on 7B and 49% on 3B. PERSISTBD retains 80% and 74% ASR, respectively, showing higher SFT persistency at both model scales. Benign RL preserves much of the attack success remaining after SFT, and the advantage of PERSISTBD remains at the final endpoint. After 150 RL steps, Base backdoor ASR is 44% on 7B and 55% on 3B, compared with 81% and 74% for PERSISTBD. Thus, residual backdoor behavior survives the full pipeline in all four random-position branches. The 7B Base backdoor shows larger increase during RL in the first-position setting: ASR rises from 51% before RL to 70% after 150 steps, compared with 41% to 44% in the random-position setting. This difference shows that the magnitude of the observed RL increase varies across triggerplacement settings. For the 7B Base backdoor, FTR remains 0% on the 100 clean counterparts throughout RL.
